deep.reconstruction:
The page is a large ruled table that continues the previous folio. Its column heads are the primes q = 97, 101, …, 223; the '9' at the far left is the clipped tail of '89' from the previous page. Thick rules divide the columns into groups: 97–113, 127–151, 157–181, 191–223. The page is split vertically into blocks of rows. Only the lowest block, for the last primes below 1000, carries entries. Its row labels are p = 953, (967), 971, 977, 983, 991, 997. The 967 label is not legible, but the spacing leaves room for that row, and two isolated dots sit in it.

A small circle in cell (p, q) means that q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. Legendre symbol (q/p) = +1. Spot checks confirm this, with the symbols computed by quadratic reciprocity (my computations):
- Row 971: (97/971) = (971/97) = (1/97) = +1, marked. (103/971) = −(971/103) = −(44/103) = −(11/103) = +1, marked. (107/971) = −(8/107) = +1, marked. (131/971) = −(54/131) = +1, marked.
- Row 971, unmarked: (101/971) = (62/101) = −1 and (109/971) = (99/109) = (11/109) = −1. Also (113/971) = (67/113) = −1, unmarked.
- Row 997: (97/997) = (27/97) = +1 and (101/997) = (88/101) = +1, both marked. (109/997) = (16/109) = +1, marked.
- Other rows: (101/991) = (82/101) = +1, marked; (113/991) = (87/113) = +1, marked; (127/977) = (88/127) = +1, marked.
- Row 967 dots: (97/967) = (94/97) = +1 and (223/967) = −(75/223) = −(3/223) = +1, so these are residues.

The straight strokes join circles in horizontally or vertically adjacent cells. They do not encode a further arithmetic relation; they are a visual device that makes runs and clusters of residues stand out. Examples: the run 101–103–107–109 in row 977; the square 103/107 × 971/977; the vertical chain under 107 from 977 down to 997.

The rows 953 and 967 are evidently unfinished. For instance (103/953) = (26/103) = (2/103)(13/103) = +1, yet that cell is blank. So the filling apparently proceeded from 997 upward. The upper blocks of the sheet, presumably for smaller p, are still empty.

Overall the sheet is part of a systematic table of quadratic characters of the primes q ≤ 359 (continued on the next folio) modulo the primes p < 1000. It extends to larger q the kind of table Gauss printed as Table II of the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae.
errors: No arithmetic errors detected in the cells spot-checked (about 15 checked against reciprocity).
Rows 953 and 967 are incomplete rather than wrong: e.g. 103 is a residue of 953 but unmarked; only two dots appear in row 967.

results.what: Table of quadratic residue characters (q/p) for primes q from 97 to 223 against primes p from 953 to 997, with residues marked by circles and adjacent marks joined by lines
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table
results.usually_credited_to: Such tables are standard; Gauss himself published a table of residues in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Table II; later Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus (1839)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine computational table of quadratic residues, of exactly the kind Gauss is known to have compiled and published (DA Table II). The only mildly notable feature is the graphical linking of adjacent residue marks.

checkable.asserts: 103 and 107 are QRs mod 971 (square corner marks)
unmarked cells in row 971 are non-residues
the horizontal chains in row 977 consist of residues
the two isolated dots belong to row 967 and mark residues
row 953 is unfinished (a residue left unmarked)

transcription_corrections: The leading '9' in the header is the clipped tail of '89' continued from the previous page.
A row for 967 lies between 953 and 971 (label not visible); it contains two dots, under 97 and 223.
The circles mark quadratic residues (q/p) = +1; the connecting lines join horizontally/vertically adjacent marked cells.
